processing: Fixed, rolled, then piled to ferment (wodui), pressed into bricks and dried; aged further in storage.
harvest_season: Not sold by a prized picking. Bricks are bought by factory and production year.
appearance_dry: Firm, dark brown to black-brown rectangular bricks, sometimes loose in the case of unpressed qing zhuan.
appearance_liquor: Red-brown to deep red and clear.
taste_profile: Mellow, thick and soft, with aged wood and earth aromas and sometimes a hint of honey.

brewing.notes: Break off a chunk and rinse it first. Clay or a sturdy gaiwan with water at or near boiling works best, and the brick can also be simmered.

vintage_note: Bought as bricks by factory and production year, and many are stored for years, with aroma growing and body softening with age. Fresh and aged bricks both sell. Chibi qing zhuan has European geographical indication protection, and Zhao Li Qiao is the name most often seen.
description:
Hubei heicha is the province's dark tea, and in practice this means qing zhuan, the green brick tea of Chibi and Xianning in southern Hubei. Chinese references group it into pressed bricks and a loose form.

The core of the process is piling: damp leaf is heaped to ferment, which gives the soft, earthy character, before steaming and pressing into hard bricks. Those bricks were made for long trade routes and are still made for ageing.

The cup is red-brown and mellow, with aged wood and earth, and sometimes some honey. Boiling water and a rinse are essential. These bricks are forgiving, and you can stretch the steeps out or simmer a piece.

Look for the producer and year on the wrapper. The UNESCO-listed Zhao Li Qiao brick-making craft is the best-known reference point, and Chibi calls itself the home of Chinese qing zhuan. Treat health claims on the packet with a pinch of salt.
history:
Qing zhuan was made in the Qing dynasty at Yangloudong in Puqi, today's Chibi, which is why it was also called Dong Zhuan. A 2024 People's Daily report places its departure along the Tea Road to Central Asia and Europe more than 300 years back; this is a commonly repeated figure, not a documented date.

The Zhao Li Qiao brick-making technique is part of China's traditional tea processing listing at UNESCO. Today producers run mechanised lines while selling into Russia and Mongolia.
